e.etymology: From Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ', from Greek Khristos, 'anointed'. Ten kings of Denmark bore it, and the pilgrim hero of Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress is named Christian.

assoc.t: Christian, a follower of Christianity

e.note: The name states a religion outright, which may matter in a non-Christian or interfaith family.

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Jackson, 'son of Jack', that spread in the 2000s along with the short form Jax.
Feminine of Valentinus, from Latin valens, 'strong, healthy'. Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963.

assoc.t: Valentina Mexican hot sauce

e.etymology: From Hebrew Channah, 'grace, favor'. In the Old Testament she is the mother of the prophet Samuel. Anna and Anne come from the same name.
namesakes: Hannah Montana (Miley Cyrus's Disney Channel pop star)

assoc.t: Hannah Montana, Miley Cyrus's Disney Channel pop star

e.etymology: From Hebrew Eli, 'ascent'. Eli was the high priest who raised the prophet Samuel. The name is also a short form of Elijah, Elias and Elisha.
From Greek Silas, from an Aramaic form of Saul, 'asked for'. Silas was Paul's missionary companion in Acts. He is also called Silvanus, so the name is often tied to Latin silva, 'forest'.
namesakes: Silas Marner (title character of the George Eliot novel)
Silas (the albino monk in The Da Vinci Code)

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Zoe, from Greek zoe, 'life'. The spelling spread in the 2000s, helped by the Nickelodeon series Zoey 101.

assoc.t: Zoey 101, the Nickelodeon teen series
Zoey, a member of Huntr/x in KPop Demon Hunters

e.etymology: From an English surname based on the medieval name Everard (Dutch Everaert), from Germanic eber, 'wild boar', plus hard, 'brave, hardy'.

assoc.t: Everett, Washington, home of a giant Boeing plant

e.etymology: From the Jordan River, Hebrew Yarden, from yarad, 'to descend, flow down'. Crusaders brought its water home for baptisms, and children were named for it.
namesakes: Jordan Peele (Get Out director and comedian)

assoc.t: Michael Jordan, basketball legend (surname)
Jordan, the Middle Eastern country, and the Jordan River
Air Jordan sneakers from Nike, called Jordans

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yehonatan, 'Yahweh has given'. In the Old Testament, Jonathan is the son of King Saul and the loyal friend of David.

assoc.t: Jonathan apple variety

e.etymology: From the English occupational surname for someone who sawed timber. Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer gave it a boyish, adventurous air.
namesakes: Sawyer (con man on the TV series Lost)

assoc.t: Tom Sawyer, Mark Twain's boy hero (surname)

e.etymology: A short form of Hebrew Mikhayahu, 'who is like Yahweh?', a close relative of Michael. Micah was a minor prophet who foretold a ruler from Bethlehem.
From Hebrew Le'ah, traditionally 'weary', though it may be related to an Akkadian word for 'cow'. Leah was Jacob's first wife and mother of six of his twelve sons.
Probably first a pet form of Elizabeth, later understood as a derivative of Latin lilium, 'lily'. It has been in use since the 16th century.

e.meaning: illusion (Sanskrit); also a form of Maia or Maria
e.etymology: Several names meet here: Sanskrit maya, 'illusion', a name of the goddess Lakshmi; a spelling of Maia, the Greek nymph who was mother of Hermes; and a short form of Maria.

assoc.t: the Maya, ancient civilization of Central America
Maya, Autodesk's 3D animation software

e.etymology: Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Leonard, from Old High German Leonhart: leo, 'lion', plus hart, 'hard, strong'.

assoc.t: Leonardo da Vinci, painter of the Mona Lisa
Leonardo, leader of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles

e.etymology: From Hebrew Delilah, usually linked to a root meaning 'weak' or 'delicate'. In the Book of Judges she betrays Samson by having his hair cut. The 2006 song Hey There Delilah fueled its revival.

assoc.t: biblical Delilah, who betrayed Samson
Hey There Delilah, the Plain White T's hit song
Delilah, the syndicated nighttime radio host
Delilah, the 1968 Tom Jones hit song

e.note: The biblical Delilah is a byword for a treacherous seductress.

e.etymology: From the English occupational surname for a fuller, who cleaned and thickened woolen cloth by treading on it.
namesakes: Paul Walker (Fast and Furious actor; surname)

assoc.t: Walker, Texas Ranger, Chuck Norris's TV lawman
walker, a mobility aid, and a baby walker

e.etymology: From Germanic Hrodebert: hrod, 'fame', plus berht, 'bright'. The Normans brought it to England, and Robert the Bruce made it a royal name in Scotland.
From Hebrew Yirmeyahu, 'Yahweh will raise up' or 'exalt'. The prophet who warned of Jerusalem's fall; his laments gave English the word jeremiad.

assoc.t: Jeremiah was a bullfrog, lyric from Joy to the World

e.etymology: From Latin augustus, 'venerable', the title of the first Roman emperor, for whom the month is named. It is the German and Scandinavian form of Augustus, and in English also a month name.
namesakes: August Pullman (Auggie, hero of the novel Wonder)

assoc.t: August, the eighth month of the year

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, 'he will add'. Written José in Spanish, it is often paired with a second name, as in José Luis or María José.

assoc.t: no way, Jose, a rhyming catchphrase
Jose Cuervo tequila

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English cola, coal, plus tun, settlement. It moved from surname to first name in the United States in the late 20th century.
namesakes: Colton Underwood (former NFL player and star of The Bachelor)
Colton Haynes (actor, Teen Wolf and Arrow)

assoc.t: city in Southern California's Inland Empire

e.meaning: from Paisley, a Scottish town whose name may mean pasture
e.etymology: From the surname taken from the town of Paisley near Glasgow, Scottish Gaelic Pàislig. The town's shawl weavers gave their name to the curved teardrop pattern called paisley.
namesakes: Brad Paisley (country music singer and guitarist)

assoc.t: paisley, the teardrop-shaped fabric pattern
town in Scotland near Glasgow

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English east plus tun, settlement: the farm or village to the east. A doublet of Aston.
namesakes: Sheena Easton (Scottish pop singer of the 1980s)

assoc.t: baseball bat and sporting goods brand
city in Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley

e.etymology: From Greek genesis, creation or origin, the title of the first book of the Bible. In American use as a given name since the 1980s and common in Spanish-speaking families as Génesis.

assoc.t: Book of Genesis, first book of the Bible
Hyundai's luxury car brand
British rock band fronted by Phil Collins
Sega Genesis, 1990s video game console

e.etymology: The Italian form of German Heinz, a pet form of Heinrich (Henry), from heim, home, and rihhi, ruler. Also a short form of Italian names ending in -enzo such as Lorenzo and Vincenzo.
namesakes: Enzo Ferrari (founder of the Ferrari car company)

assoc.t: Ferrari Enzo, supercar named for the company's founder

e.etymology: A short form of Theodore, from Greek theos, god, and doron, gift; also short for Theodora, Theobald and other Theo- names. Now common as a full name.
namesakes: Theo Huxtable (the son on The Cosby Show)
Theo James (actor, Divergent and The White Lotus)

e.etymology: A patronymic surname from Addie, a medieval pet form of Adam, plus -son. It became a popular girls' name in the 2000s, following Alison and Madison.
namesakes: Addison Rae (TikTok star turned pop singer)
Addison Montgomery (doctor on Grey's Anatomy and Private Practice)

assoc.t: Addison's disease, an adrenal gland disorder
Addison Montgomery of Grey's Anatomy

e.etymology: From an English surname taken from place names, Old English lang, long, plus dun, hill.
namesakes: Michael Landon (actor, Little House on the Prairie)

e.etymology: Usually linked to Gael, the word for a Gaelic-speaking Celt, from Old Irish Goídel. The Breton name Gaël may instead be a contraction of Gwenaël or Judicaël. In the US it is mostly used by Spanish-speaking families.
namesakes: Gael García Bernal (Mexican actor, Y Tu Mamá También and Coco)

e.etymology: From the English and Scottish occupational surname for a huntsman, itself the ordinary word. It became a common first name in the United States in the 1990s.
namesakes: Hunter S. Thompson (gonzo journalist, Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas)
Hunter Biden (son of President Joe Biden)

assoc.t: Hunter, British rain boot brand
Hunter ceiling fans
